name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++ in AI: The Performance Layer Beneath Python
answer: C++ is a compiled, general purpose programming language first released in 1985 and standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21. In AI work it is the performance layer beneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it buys speed and memory control at the cost of a steeper learning curve and manual resource management, so it is usually reached for when Python is too slow or too heavy.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled programming language whose first release was in 1985, maintained under the stewardship of the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee, with isocpp.org as its official site. Within AI it occupies the performance layer underneath the Python surface. PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written in C++. The site's standardization pages show a language under continuous revision, with the committee completing technical work on C++26 in March 2026 and voting the first additions into the working draft for C++29 in June 2026. It is not a framework or a library but the substrate on which much of the numerical and runtime machinery of AI is built.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The facts place C++ in training and inference infrastructure, in CUDA kernels, and in inference runtimes such as llama.cpp. Its strength is operating under real space and time constraints, which the site's CppCon 2026 keynote description ties to sustained industry demand for programmers who can work at that level. The site also documents a machine learning study group, SG19, meeting regularly, and a low latency, games, embedded and financial trading group, SG14, which indicates where the language is expected to stay strongest. Where it is the best choice is where latency, memory footprint or throughput dominate, and where Python would add overhead the application cannot absorb.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The official material does not present a beginner curriculum, and the facts do not describe a learning path, so the difficulty must be inferred from what the site does show. The standardization pages assume familiarity with compiler flags, modules, undefined behavior and proposals, and the CppCon talk coverage assumes an audience comfortable with metaprogramming and benchmarking. A reader should expect to need programming fundamentals and some systems knowledge before the language's AI uses make sense. What the site offers a newcomer is the annual developer survey, described as a ten minute one pager, plus conference registration and blog posts, rather than a structured tutorial.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site documents an active community around the language. There is an annual global C++ developer survey whose results are posted publicly and shared with committee participants and tool vendors, with a 145 page 2026 report including all write-in responses. There are regular mailings of new standards papers, meeting minutes for SG14 and SG19, and trip reports from ISO meetings in Kona, Varna and Brno. CppCon runs annually, with CppCon 2026 starting September 12 in Aurora, Colorado. Compiler support is tracked through release news, including GCC 16.1 with C++26 reflection, contracts and safety hardening. The facts list no tracked repositories, so the site's own pages are the record here.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: C++ is built for speed and memory control rather than for quick experiments, and the site's coverage reflects that emphasis. C++26 is described as bringing reflection, an initial round of memory safety hardening, and standard library performance enhancers such as std::simd and std::execution. A CppCon 2025 talk describes using an experimental Bloomberg LLVM fork with reflective metaprogramming to parse JSON directly into C++ structures, with tests, benchmarks and documentation. The cost of this orientation is that iteration is slower and more deliberate than in a scripting language, and the site does not claim otherwise. The facts do not describe a REPL or notebook style workflow.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site cites SlashData and IDC data documenting sustained growth in demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that can operate under real space and time constraints. The facts place C++ beneath PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA and most inference runtimes, which indicates deep adoption in AI infrastructure rather than in application level AI scripting. The site does not present C++ as a legacy choice, and the standardization activity through C++26 and C++29 supports that. For someone choosing it for work, the reasonable reading of these facts is that it is a current standard in performance critical roles, while the site does not quantify salaries or job counts.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: The pattern the facts describe is polyglot. C++ sits below Python, which remains the surface most AI practitioners write against, and it is the language in which the underlying engines and kernels are implemented. The site's own material is largely about the language in isolation, its standards process, its compilers and its conferences, and it does not lay out integration guides for Python or other languages. What can be said from the facts is that C++ is typically used with the frameworks it underpins rather than instead of them, and that a developer working in AI is more likely to meet it in a runtime, a kernel or a serving path than as the first language of a project.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about work in progress. Undefined behavior is being catalogued in a new annex in the C++29 working draft, described as a first step toward addressing it systematically, and draft profiles for stronger portable memory safety guarantees are still being prototyped. C++20 modules support in GCC 16.1 is still experimental and must be enabled with a flag. A blog post by Giovanni Dicanio recounts an AI review of his WinReg library that reported zero length bugs, a reminder that generated analysis needs checking. The official material does not say how quickly these features will ship, how widely profiles will be adopted, or what C++ should be used for in AI beyond the runtime and kernel roles the facts already name.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
